_meta.purpose: Rejecting postings that are not real, applyable vacancies — T030c.
_meta.two_separate_judgements: Junk and fraud are kept apart and never merged into one 'suspicious' score. Junk means there is no posting behind the row — an error page, a test record, a placeholder. Fraud means there is a posting and it is trying to take something from the applicant. They have different evidence, different false-positive costs and different consequences, and a reviewer reading a rejection needs to know which one fired.
_meta.logging_rule: Every rejection writes a `rejection` row naming the rule and quoting the matched text. Nothing is silently dropped, and nothing is deleted — disable a rule here and re-run to get those postings back.
_meta.measured_against_corpus: Calibrated against the 4,402 postings in data/jobfinder.db on 2026-09-23, not invented. Findings that shaped these rules: (1) short titles are NOT junk — 'SDR', 'Sales', 'Recruiter', 'Porter', 'barista', 'Labourers' are all real vacancies, so there is deliberately no minimum-length rule; (2) the word 'whatsapp' appears in 8 postings and ALL 8 are legitimate — Aircall, Superchat, Careem and Airbnb build messaging products, and a recruiter lists it as an outreach channel. A bare keyword rule would have been 8/8 false positives, which is why every fraud signal below is phrase-shaped and requires the word to sit in a construction that names the ASK.
_meta.expected_yield_note: On this corpus these rules are expected to reject a handful of junk rows and approximately zero fraud. That is the correct result, not a broken ruleset: the corpus comes from Greenhouse, Lever, RemoteOK and Arbeitnow, which curate their sources. The fraud rules exist for the freelance and marketplace sources added in T031b, which is where advance-fee scams actually live.

junk.match_rule: Junk patterns are matched against the WHOLE normalised title, anchored, never as a substring. '404' as a substring would reject 'Room 404 Facilities Technician'.

rules.label: The title is an error string, a test record or a placeholder, not a job
rules.corpus_evidence: Matches 'Oops something happened', 'CHECK BACK SOON', '404', 'Test', 'test', 'test Copy' and '12650000' in data/jobfinder.db. The legacy engine scored 'Oops something happened' at 61.14 and would have generated an application for it.
rules.false_positive_risk: LOW. Anchored whole-title match, so a real title containing one of these words is untouched.

rules.label: The posting is a catch-all, not a role that can be applied to
rules.rationale: These are real entries posted by real employers, so they are not fraud. They are still not applyable: there is no role to tailor a CV to and no requirement set to check sufficiency against, so generating an application for one produces a document addressed to nothing.
rules.separately_disableable: Kept as its own rule precisely because a user who wants to send speculative applications can turn this one off without losing J01.

fraud.match_rule: Fraud is a weighted judgement, not a single keyword. Signals are summed and the posting is rejected only at or above `reject_at`. Every signal that fired is recorded, so a rejection can be read back as an argument rather than a verdict.
fraud.reject_at_note: A threshold, so it lives here and not in code (I-23). At 1.0 any single `strong` signal rejects on its own, and two `medium` signals reject together. A lone `medium` or `weak` signal flags in the evidence but does not reject.

signals.label: The applicant is asked for money
signals.rationale: A legitimate employer never charges to be hired. This is the defining shape of the advance-fee job scam.
signals.measured_false_positive_control: MEASURED, and this signal was rewritten because of it. The first version matched the bare noun — 'placement fee', 'processing fee' — and rejected 4 real vacancies in data/jobfinder.db: two Samsara sales roles whose copy says candidates should want more than 'a placement fee or a quarterly target', and a Spotify FP&A role that forecasts 'processing fees, vendor mix, and refunds'. Every pattern now requires the applicant to be named as the PAYER, not the word to be present. REWRITTEN AGAIN after the first live run (2026-09-24). The note above said every pattern named the applicant as payer; the third did not — bare 'pay a fee' — and it fired on Airbnb's anti-scam notice (155 postings) and on ABS declining to pay recruitment agencies. It now requires 'you', 'candidate' or 'applicant' in the same clause, and every signal passes the negation guard.
signals.false_positive_risk: LOW after the rewrite. A finance or payments role discusses fees as a subject; a scam addresses them to the reader.

signals.label: Money routed to or from the applicant through an untraceable rail
signals.rationale: These rails are chosen because they cannot be reversed. A payroll does not run on gift cards.
signals.measured_false_positive_control: MEASURED, and rewritten. The first version matched 'gift card' and 'crypto payment' as nouns and rejected 4 real vacancies: three Stripe roles and an Airbnb loyalty role. Those companies BUILD gift-card and crypto payment products, so the nouns are their subject matter. Every pattern now requires a transfer construction with the applicant at one end.

signals.label: Identity or banking documents demanded up front
signals.rationale: Identity and bank details are collected after an offer, by an employer who already exists. Asking at application is harvesting.
signals.cross_reference: The same documents Jarvis itself stores as `restricted` and never reads (I-13). A posting demanding them is asking for precisely what the system refuses to expose.

signals.label: Applications accepted only through a personal messaging account
signals.rationale: An employer with a real hiring process has an address at its own domain. Routing applicants to a consumer messenger keeps the recruiter unidentifiable and the exchange off any record.
signals.measured_false_positive_control: MEASURED. A bare 'whatsapp' match would have flagged 8 of 8 legitimate postings in data/jobfinder.db — Aircall, Superchat, Careem, Airbnb and a recruiter describing outreach channels. Requiring the apply-here construction drops all 8.
signals.strength_rationale: Medium, not strong: a small agency genuinely does recruit over WhatsApp in some markets. On its own it flags; with any second signal it rejects.

signals.label: Unrealistic earnings promised with no experience or no interview
signals.rationale: Pairs an outsized promise with the removal of every step that would let the employer check the applicant — the combination, not either half.
signals.false_positive_risk: MEDIUM. Genuine entry-level and commission roles use some of this language, which is why it is medium and pairs with S04/S06 rather than rejecting alone.

signals.label: Applications go to a free consumer mailbox rather than a company domain
signals.rationale: Weak on its own — a genuine sole trader or a very small employer may have no domain, and rejecting them would cut exactly the small businesses this user wants to reach. It is a corroborating signal, never a verdict.
signals.false_positive_risk: HIGH alone, which is why it is weighted 0.25 and cannot reject by itself.

basis: A signal match is ignored when a negation appears earlier in the SAME CLAUSE.
Measured on the first live discovery run, 2026-09-24: 155 of Airbnb's 160
postings were rejected as fraud on the sentence "We'll also never ask you to
pay a fee, send money, deposit or cash a check" — Airbnb's own anti-scam
notice. Employers add that paragraph because of recruitment fraud, so the
unguarded rule hid the most careful employers. An ABS posting went the same
way on "ABS will not pay a fee to any third-party agency".
The clause bound is the part that keeps the guard from becoming a bypass:
"Don't worry, you must pay a registration fee" still rejects, because the
comma ends the clause holding the negation. A sentence-wide window would let
any scam that opens with a reassurance straight through.
